16.0.0.en: After the great victory that Samson achieved over the Philistines who wanted to seize him, he became feared in all the five great Philistine cities, so he would enter and leave them without anyone daring to molest him. On one of his visits to the city of Gaza, the greatest of the Philistine cities, desire was stirred in his heart when he saw, or heard of, a harlot, and he went into her house to sin with her. This shows two things:

16.0.1.en: 1- The importance of being on guard after victory against the devil, because he devises snares for us, and the matter needs greater exactness and holding fast to God's commandments.

16.0.2.en: 2- The Holy Bible shows the virtues of the saints and their sins so that we too may be encouraged if we sin and repent, for repentance turns fornicators and sinners into saints.

16.0.3.en: Concentrate on your aim in life, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, for when Samson neglected his aim, namely the salvation of his people, he was drawn away by the desire for women, and his enemies overpowered him, as will appear later. Remind yourself at the beginning of every day of your aim, so that if you are distracted from it you return to it quickly.

16.1.0.en: The Philistines in Gaza heard that Samson had come to their city, and the desire to take vengeance on him awoke again in their souls. So they surrounded the house in which he was staying, while another group of them encamped at the gate of the city so that he would not go out by it, and they waited in silence until morning to seize him.

16.2.0.en: Contrary to the expectation of the people of Gaza, Samson arose in the middle of the night and came to the gate of the city while everyone was asleep, and pulled out the gate with its two leaves, its two posts and its bar, and put the whole on his shoulders and went up to one of the mountains facing the city of Hebron, that is, he headed for a mountain lying between the cities of Gaza and Hebron, and threw the uprooted gate on the mountain and went his way.

16.2.1.en: If the Philistines boasted of their bodily strength, which appeared afterward in the form of Goliath the giant (1 Sam 17), God sends them a person from His people stronger than all their imaginings, that perhaps they might believe in God and reject their idols.

16.3.0.en: The valley of Sorek: a valley that begins 21 km west of Jerusalem and extends to the Mediterranean Sea (map 10). Delilah: a name meaning pampered.

16.3.1.en: For the third time Samson falls into the snare of a pagan woman, whose name was Delilah, a Philistine woman from the valley of Sorek.

16.4.0.en: The shekel of silver: equal to about 15 grams.

16.4.1.en: "See wherein his great strength lieth, and by what means we may prevail against him": learn from him the secret of his extraordinary strength and how we can overpower him and overcome him.

16.4.2.en: The Philistines were waiting for an opportunity to take vengeance on Samson, and when they learned of his attachment to Delilah, and they thought that Samson carried exceptional strength as the result of a magical work which, if annulled, would make him lose his strength and become an ordinary man who could be controlled, five of their chiefs went to Delilah and persuaded her to show him affection and coax him until she learned from him the secret of his strength, and each of them would give her, as a reward for this service of hers, a thousand shekels of silver.

16.5.0.en: Delilah yielded to the Philistines' demand of her and asked Samson about the source of his strength and with what he could be bound so that he could be controlled.

16.6.0.en: "Withs" (cords): they were mostly made from the intestines of animals.

16.6.1.en: Samson told her that his strength would depart and he would become like any ordinary man if he were bound with seven fresh cords. Of course this was a lie, because he knew that Delilah might reveal his secret to the Philistines, for he had been deceived before by his first wife, the Philistine of Timnath, when she revealed the solution of the riddle; so he deceived Delilah and continued with her to enjoy his desire. And this is a great error, for a person to make light of the devil's wars; he should have fled from the passions and so saved himself from what would happen to him when the Philistines seized him.

16.6.2.en: Sin draws on to other sins, for because Samson submitted to the desire of fornication, he also allowed himself lying. If only you would be careful and cut off sin from its beginning by repentance and keeping away from its sources, lest it draw you on to other sins.

16.7.0.en: Delilah passed on to the chiefs of the Philistines what Samson had told her, and they prepared for her seven cords with which she bound him tightly, perhaps while he was asleep by the effect of a drug.

16.8.0.en: "A thread of tow": the weak threads left over after the spinning of flax, which are not fit to be twisted to form strong threads, but can be used in lamps for light.

16.8.1.en: The Philistines were hiding in Samson's house until Delilah should bind him with the cords, and when she finished binding him she called to him, saying: The Philistines are upon thee, Samson. He awoke from his sleep and broke the cords as a thread of tow is broken, for what Samson had said about the secret of his strength was a deception, so they had not yet arrived at the secret.

16.9.0.en: "Behold, thou hast mocked me": behold, you have deceived me.

16.9.1.en: Delilah reproached him for deceiving her and lying to her, and repeated to him the same question, that is, with what he could be bound so that his strength would depart.

16.10.0.en: When she pressed him for the second time, he told her that his strength would depart if he were bound with new ropes which had not yet been used.

16.11.0.en: Delilah believed him this time also and bound him with new ropes as he said, and the Philistines were hiding in the house as happened the first time, waiting for the signal to come out of their hiding place and seize him. When Delilah cried out, saying as the previous time, "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson," Samson arose and broke the new ropes as though they were a thin thread.

16.12.0.en: "The web": the lengthwise threads on the loom, as distinct from the weft, which is the crosswise threads.

16.12.1.en: The scene was repeated for the third time, for the woman came back again and repeated to him her reproach for deceiving her, and asked him not to repeat what he had done but to be truthful this time and tell her with what and how he might be bound so that his strength would be weakened. So he told her that this would be if she wove the seven locks of his head with the web and fastened them with the pin (v. 14). Samson had braided his hair in seven braids. And the number "7" signifies perfection, and in this he was exact in the outward signs of the vow, but he was careless in what is more important, the evil desires.

16.13.0.en: "The pin": a piece of wood fixed in the ground to which the ropes of the tent are tied; what is meant by it here may be the lengthwise or horizontal beam of the loom, made of wood.

16.13.1.en: Delilah did what he told her, and his hair became fixed and interwoven with the threads as though it were of the same fabric, and Delilah was not content with that but, to make the binding firmer still, bound his locks and the threads of the fabric most tightly to the pin of the loom. And when she finished that she cried out, "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson," and Samson awoke from his sleep and pulled the pin from the loom and broke the threads of the fabric.

16.13.2.en: We marvel here at Samson's continuing in Delilah's hands while knowing that she wanted to reveal his secret to the Philistines, as his wife in Timnath had done, but he submitted because the desire had gained mastery over him, and he kept parleying with her so as not to lose his enjoyment of fornication. Perhaps in pride he trusted in his ability to parley and lie, but unfortunately he fell in the end into the hands of the Philistines because he did not flee for his life from sin but was careless and parleyed with it.

16.14.0.en: Delilah was angry and told him that he claimed to love her but did not prove it in practice, for he had deceived her three times and had not told her the secret of his strength, so where was that love he claimed ... And Delilah did not despair but continued to press him and kept troubling him with word and deed, until his soul could no longer bear more pressure from her, for his distress reached a great degree, until he was close to death.

16.15.0.en: "He told her all his heart": he confided his secret to her.

16.15.1.en: "There hath not come a razor upon mine head": he had not shaved the hair of his head since his birth.

16.15.2.en: At last Samson weakened before Delilah and was not able to go on keeping the secret, so he revealed to her the secret of his strength, telling her that he was a Nazarite of the Lord (that is, consecrated to the Lord), and one of the conditions of the vow was that no razor come upon his head; if his hair were shaved, his strength would leave him, for by this he would have departed from his vow and turned back from his covenant with God.

16.15.3.en: We must beware in any special relationship we form with others that it not be a cause of corrupting our spirituality and turning us aside from the path of our salvation. Let us flee for our lives from every relationship that binds us with bonds we may not be able to break free from, so that we remain captives to them, as happened with Samson, whose bodily inclinations gained mastery over his conduct and cast him into perils that could have been avoided if he had been able to free himself from them.

16.16.1.en: Delilah felt that she had succeeded this time in drawing him on to reveal his secret, and that he had been truthful in disclosing it to her, so she sent to the Philistines, assuring them that this time was not like the previous ones and that she had indeed obtained from him the secret of his strength, and they went to her with the reward they had promised her.

16.17.0.en: Perhaps this was from the effect of an intoxicating drink such as wine that was offered to him, for he slept unconscious on Delilah's knees, and she called a man who cut off the seven locks of his hair. And when he returned to consciousness signs of weakness appeared on him, and Delilah began to mock him and scoff at him, since she realized that his strength had left him.

16.18.0.en: "Shake myself": rise from the heedlessness of sleep.

16.18.1.en: She told him, as in the previous times, that the Philistines were upon him; she said it knowing perfectly well that his strength had gone, so Samson awoke from his heedlessness and said to himself, I will rise and face the Philistines, as he had done every time, and he did not realize that the Lord had left him and that he had lost the secret of his strength. So he rose by his own strength and not by the strength of God, and therefore the Philistines seized him easily.

16.19.0.en: The Philistines were able to seize him easily because he had become weak, and they put out his eyes and led him to their city Gaza and bound him with chains as is done with captives. And to humble him they used him to grind grain at the mill like animals and slaves. Thus the mighty man became humbled, his eyes gouged out, and they treated him like an animal.

16.20.0.en: With the passing of days while he was in his prison, the hair of his head began to grow little by little, which led him to remember his state as a Nazarite, and he began to realize what his condition had come to as a result of his errors, and he began to return to God in repentance.

16.21.0.en: Dagon: a pagan god of the Philistines, with the head of a man and the body of a fish.

16.21.1.en: The Philistines decided to hold a celebration for their god "Dagon" because they believed that it was he who had helped them to seize their enemy Samson, so they sacrificed a sacrifice of thanksgiving to him, expressing their happiness and gratitude to him.

16.22.0.en: They led Samson in a procession among the people gathered in the temple, a captive bound in chains to the utmost of humiliating him, praising their god and saying that it was he who gave them victory over their enemy Samson who had wronged them, for he had burned their fields and killed many of them, and then they brought him back to the prison attached to the temple.

16.23.0.en: "When their hearts were merry": they indulged in eating, drinking and revelry.

16.23.1.en: As is the custom of pagan peoples in their celebrations, they joined them with the drinking of much wine and revelry. When their minds were affected by the wine, an idea occurred to them which they carried out at once, namely to summon Samson into their midst to perform some acrobatic movements, to the utmost of mocking him, and they made him stand between the pillars of the entrance, so that everyone outside the gates of the temple and also those inside it could see him.

16.24.0.en: Samson asked the boy charged with holding his hand to lead him, to take him to the main pillars on which the temple rests so that he might lean on them, after he showed weariness from much playing, and the boy granted his request.

16.25.0.en: The temple was full of thousands of men and women of the Philistines, and because the temple was filled with spectators, three thousand of them stood on its roof so as to be able to see Samson as he played like a buffoon. The chiefs of the Philistines were also present at this celebration.

16.26.0.en: Samson prayed to God and entreated Him, hoping that He would not forsake him because of his sin, and that He would remember him as His son and not leave him because of his thoughtlessness and folly. And he asked God to restore his strength to him, and give it back to him if only once, in which he might take vengeance on the Philistines who had humbled him and put out his eyes, and strike them a blow greater than any previous blow of his against them.

16.27.0.en: Samson put his hands on the two foundation pillars on which the building of the temple rested, which were near each other, so his right hand was on one pillar and his left on the other pillar.

16.28.0.en: Samson knew that if he lived after this event of pulling down the temple, the Philistines would make an example of him more and more, and torture him and then kill him; therefore he asked God to help him take vengeance on the Philistines in order to free his people from their occupation and their humbling of them, even if the price were his death with them. Then he leaned on the two pillars with force, as though pushing them apart from each other, and the Lord answered his prayer and accepted his repentance and gave him strength anew, so the pillars of the temple were shaken and it fell on those in it, and a very great number of the Philistines were killed, more than he had killed in his previous battles with them, and their chiefs also fell dead in their midst.

16.28.1.en: Thus Samson died a martyr in faith in God, sacrificing his life to rescue his people, and the Apostle Paul bore witness of him that he is among the heroes of faith (Heb 11:33). He is a type of Christ, who cast out many demons in His life on earth, but by His death bound all the demons.

16.29.0.en: His relatives and the sons of his clan came to Gaza and carried his body and returned with it to his birthplace, in his town "Zorah" (ch. 13:2), and buried him in the tomb of his father, lying between Zorah and Eshtaol (ch. 13:25). The period during which he judged the children of Israel was twenty years, during which he broke the power of the Philistines and restrained their domination over his people.

16.29.1.en: The door of repentance is open to you however much sin has humbled you, for God loves you and is ready to forgive you however grievous your sins, and even restores your strength to you and gives you authority over your enemies the demons.

16.29.2.en: The miracles of Samson (1) Killing the lion on his way to Timnath (ch. 14:5). (2) Killing thirty of the Philistines at Ashkelon (ch. 14:19). (3) Catching three hundred jackals and burning the fields of the Philistines (ch. 15:4). (4) Breaking the new ropes and killing a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass (ch. 15:13-15). (5) Pulling up the gate of the city of Gaza with its two posts and its leaves, carrying it and going up with it onto the mountain (ch. 16:3). (6) The Lord brings water out of the hollow for him and he drinks (ch. 15:19). (7) Breaking the seven cords, and the new ropes, and pulling out the loom with its pin in Delilah's house (ch. 16:9, 12, 14).

16.29.3.en: (8) Bringing down the temple of Dagon and killing the Philistines (ch. 16:30). Points of likeness between Samson and the Lord Jesus Christ (1) The birth of each by heavenly good tidings (ch. 13:3, Lk 1:31). (2) The birth of each by a miracle, for Samson was born of a barren woman, and Jesus of a virgin girl (ch. 13:2, Lk 1:27). (3) The Lord declared that Samson would begin to deliver his people (ch. 13:5), and the Lord Jesus' name means Savior, and He saved His people by redeeming them on the Cross (Lk 2:11). (4) The Spirit of the Lord moved Samson (ch. 13:25), and with the Lord Jesus the Spirit led Him (Lk 4:1). But there is a difference in the two cases, for the moving of Samson by the Spirit of the Lord means guiding him, while with the Lord Jesus the Spirit's moving Him means His carrying out the eternal plan that God devised for the redemption of mankind. (5) Samson was able to overcome his enemies, and the Lord Jesus overcame the devil, sin, death and the world by the Cross.

16.29.4.en: (6) Samson was delivered to his enemies by a group of his own kin and of his tribe Judah (ch. 15:13, 14), and the Lord Jesus was delivered by His disciple Judas to the Jews.

16.29.5.en: (7) Samson did great deeds alone without the help of soldiers or companions, and Christ accomplished salvation alone.

16.29.6.en: (8) When Samson fell into the hands of the Philistines they put out his eyes so that he would not see, and when the Jews seized Christ they blindfolded His eyes and struck Him.

16.29.7.en: (9) Each of them prayed at his death, but Samson's prayer was for vengeance on his enemies, while Christ prayed to forgive those who crucified Him.

16.29.8.en: (10) With the death of Samson his enemies died with him, and Christ buried sin by His death.

16.29.9.en: Points of difference between Samson and the Lord Jesus (1) Samson's life was full of human weakness and errors, while Christ is the Holy Lord alone (1 Pet 2:22). (2) Samson's struggle was bodily against the Philistines, while Christ's wrestling was spiritual against the devil and the powers of evil.

16.29.10.en: (3) Samson declared that he was doing wrong to the Philistines because they had done wrong to him (ch. 15:5), while Christ did not take vengeance on those who opposed Him (1 Pet 2:23). (4) At Samson's death he asked God to take vengeance on his enemies (ch. 16:28), while Christ at His death asked forgiveness for those who opposed Him (Lk 23:34). (5) Samson's deliverance of his people was a material deliverance from the Philistines, while Christ's deliverance is salvation from eternal perdition and the wrath of God.

16.29.11.en: (6) Samson delivered only his people, while Christ proclaimed salvation to the whole world.

16.29.12.en: (7) Samson's deliverance of his people was incomplete and temporary, and after him Samuel and David played a part in fighting the Philistines, while Christ completed the free salvation to the full, alone.
